paragraphs.heading: A dam for the tides
paragraphs.text: A tidal barrage is a structure like a dam, built across a bay or river, that captures energy from water flowing in and out with the tides. Unlike an ordinary dam, which holds water back on one side, it lets the sea in at high tide and lets it out at low tide. Operators track the tidal flow and open or close sluice gates at key moments in the tidal cycle. Turbines sit at these sluices and make power as the water moves through.

paragraphs.heading: The parts of a barrage
paragraphs.text: It works much like a hydro dam that produces head, a height difference in water that creates pressure. Whenever the water level outside the basin differs from the level inside, the turbines can generate. The main parts are caissons, sluices, turbines, ship locks and embankments. Caissons are very large concrete blocks that house the sluices, turbines and ship locks, and embankments seal the basin wherever caissons do not.

paragraphs.heading: One cycle, step by step
paragraphs.text: The basin fills through the sluices until high tide, and then the sluice gates shut; at this point extra water may be pumped in. The turbine gates stay shut until the sea falls enough to build a large head across the barrage. Then they open and the turbines run until the head is small again. The sluices reopen, the turbines are disconnected, the basin refills, and the cycle repeats with the tides.

paragraphs.heading: Filling, emptying and pumping
paragraphs.text: Ebb generation is also known as outflow generation. Making power while the basin fills, through the turbines on the rising tide, is generally much less efficient than ebb generation. The upper half of the basin holds more water than the lower half, so the level difference between basin and sea shrinks faster. Rivers flowing into the basin can cut the energy further, though a lagoon with no river inflow avoids that. Turbines can also run in reverse on spare grid power to pump the basin higher at high tide, and much of that energy comes back because output depends strongly on head: water raised 2 ft on a 10 ft tide stands 12 ft higher at low tide.

paragraphs.heading: Two basins
paragraphs.text: Some designs use two basins: one fills at high tide, the other empties at low tide, and turbines sit between them. This lets operators shift the timing of generation freely and produce power almost without a break. In ordinary estuaries, though, the extra length of barrage makes two-basin schemes very expensive. Some places do have a shape that suits them well.

paragraphs.heading: Barrages around the world
paragraphs.text: Tide mills were developed as early as the sixth century, making barrages one of the oldest ways to draw power from the tides. France's 240 MW Rance Tidal Power Station opened in November 1966 and was the world's largest tidal barrage for 45 years, until South Korea's 254 MW Sihwa Lake plant was commissioned in 2011. Smaller plants include Annapolis Royal on the Bay of Fundy and the 1.7 megawatt station at Kislaya Guba in Russia. There are few other examples. Barrages need costly civil works, and as awareness of the environment has grown, people have opposed them for changing large ecosystems that are home to many species.
